title: How to Stop Doomscrolling Without Quitting Your Phone

copy.cover_headline: Your jaw is tight and you're still scrolling

points.headline: Doomscrolling is a feeling, not a time
points.body: It's scrolling distressing content after it starts making you feel worse. Twenty minutes of cooking videos usually isn't it. Four tense minutes on a disaster thread is.

points.headline: Your body notices first
points.body: A clenched jaw. Shoulders creeping up. Shallow breath, or holding it. Refreshing a page you just refreshed. Any one of these is your cue to pause.

points.headline: The 30-second reset
points.body: Thumb off the screen, eyes on something farther away. Breathe in through your nose for 4, out slowly for 6. Three breaths, about 30 seconds. Or take one to three physiological sighs.

points.headline: Then choose on purpose
points.body: Ask: do I want more of this right now? Keep going knowingly, switch to something calmer, or close the app. Any of the three is fine, as long as it's a choice and not momentum.

points.headline: Keep it gentle
points.body: Let the air go rather than pushing it out. Stop and breathe normally if you feel dizzy, lightheaded or tingly. Don't keep sighing back to back.

copy.instagram_caption:
Willpower asks the most wound-up version of you to make the calmest decision of the day.

A newspaper ends. Infinite scroll doesn't. And in a study of about 105,000 news headline variations, each extra negative word raised click-through by about 2.3%. So the problem is the feed, not you.

That's why we prefer a reset to a rule. A ban asks you to never get wound up. A short pause meets you once you already are, which is when you actually need help.

An honest note: most research linking doomscrolling to lower well-being is correlational. It shows a connection, not a direction. You don't need a causal study to notice you feel worse after twenty minutes of bad news, though.

Breathing and pauses can help you feel calmer in the moment, but they don't replace real support. If checking the news keeps feeding your worry or getting in the way of sleep, talk to a doctor or mental health professional.

copy.facebook_message:
Most advice about doomscrolling targets minutes. But the real problem is a state: the point where the feed has wound you up and you keep going anyway.

So meet that moment instead of trying to ban it. When you notice a tight jaw, raised shoulders or shallow breath, take your thumb off the screen and look up. Breathe in through your nose for 4 and out slowly for 6, three times. That's about 30 seconds. Then ask whether you want more of this right now, and choose on purpose.

Keep it gentle, and stop if you feel dizzy.
